prompt: The law of supply states that, all else equal, there is a ___ relationship between the price of a good and the quantity supplied.

options.label: A
options.text: Neutral — price and quantity supplied are unrelated

options.label: B
options.text: Negative — as price rises, producers reduce output

options.label: C
options.text: Positive — as price rises, quantity supplied also rises

options.label: D
options.text: Inverse — as price rises, quantity supplied falls

options.label: E
options.text: Proportional — a 10% rise in price always causes exactly a 10% rise in quantity supplied

explanation: The law of supply describes a positive (direct) relationship between price and quantity supplied: when price rises, producers are willing and able to supply more; when price falls, they supply less, all else equal.

prompt: Which of the following correctly describes the shape of a supply curve on a standard price-quantity graph?

options.label: A
options.text: A vertical line, indicating that price has no effect on quantity supplied

options.label: B
options.text: Upward-sloping from left to right, reflecting the positive price-quantity relationship

options.label: C
options.text: U-shaped, reflecting increasing then decreasing returns to production

options.label: D
options.text: A horizontal line, indicating that quantity supplied never changes

options.label: E
options.text: Downward-sloping from left to right, reflecting the inverse price-quantity relationship

explanation: The supply curve is upward-sloping; as price rises (moving up the vertical axis), producers find it more profitable to increase production, so quantity supplied rises (moving right along the horizontal axis).

prompt: When the price of wheat rises from $4 to $6 per bushel, farmers plant more acres and supply more wheat. This outcome best illustrates

options.label: A
options.text: An improvement in agricultural technology that shifts supply outward

options.label: B
options.text: A change in the cost of wheat inputs that increases supply

options.label: C
options.text: A rightward shift of the supply curve for wheat

options.label: D
options.text: A leftward shift of the supply curve for wheat

options.label: E
options.text: A movement upward along supply as quantity supplied rises

explanation: A change in the price of a good causes a movement along the existing supply curve - not a shift. A higher price makes production more profitable, inducing producers to supply more; this is an increase in quantity supplied (a movement up and to the right along the curve).

prompt: A change in which of the following causes a movement along the supply curve rather than a shift of the supply curve?

options.label: A
options.text: The technology available to producers

options.label: B
options.text: The price of the good itself

options.label: C
options.text: Producer expectations about future prices

options.label: D
options.text: The price of inputs used in production

options.label: E
options.text: The number of sellers in the market

explanation: Only a change in the price of the good itself causes a movement along the supply curve (a change in quantity supplied). All other factors - input prices, technology, number of sellers, expectations, taxes/subsidies - are non-price determinants that shift the entire supply curve.

prompt: Which of the following would cause the supply curve for automobiles to shift to the RIGHT (increase in supply)?

options.label: A
options.text: A new government regulation requiring more expensive safety equipment in all vehicles

options.label: B
options.text: An improvement in robotic assembly technology that reduces production costs

options.label: C
options.text: A decrease in the number of automobile manufacturers

options.label: D
options.text: An increase in the price of steel (a key input for automobiles)

options.label: E
options.text: An increase in the price of automobiles

explanation: A technological improvement that reduces production costs is a supply determinant. Lower costs make it more profitable to produce at every price, so producers supply more - shifting the supply curve rightward; A price change would cause a movement along the curve, not a shift.

prompt: Which of the following would cause the supply curve for restaurant meals to shift to the LEFT (decrease in supply)?

options.label: A
options.text: An improvement in kitchen equipment technology

options.label: B
options.text: A significant rise in wages paid to restaurant workers (a key input)

options.text: A decrease in the price of food ingredients

options.label: D
options.text: A decrease in the price of restaurant meals

options.label: E
options.text: An increase in the number of restaurants opening in the market

explanation: Wages are an input cost for restaurants; when wages rise, production costs increase, making it less profitable to produce restaurant meals at every given price; producers supply less at every price - the supply curve shifts leftward (decreases).

prompt: Input prices are considered a determinant of supply. Which of the following is the best example of an input price change that would shift the supply of bread?

options.label: A
options.text: A rise in the price of bread at grocery stores

options.label: D
options.text: A change in consumer preferences toward whole-grain bread

options.label: E
options.text: An increase in the number of bread consumers

explanation: Flour is an input in bread production. A rise in the price of flour increases the cost of producing bread, reducing profitability at every price and shifting the supply curve for bread leftward; this is a change in an input price - a supply determinant.

prompt: A technological improvement that reduces the cost of producing solar panels is best described as causing

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: A leftward shift of the supply curve for solar panels

options.text: An increase in the price of solar panels

options.text: A movement up along the supply curve for solar panels

explanation: Improved technology that reduces production costs is a supply determinant; lower costs allow producers to profitably supply more solar panels at every price level, shifting the supply curve rightward (increasing supply).

prompt: When the number of sellers in a market increases, the market supply curve will most likely

options.label: A
options.text: Supply shifts left

options.label: B
options.text: Supply becomes horizontal

options.label: C
options.text: Supply remains unchanged

options.label: D
options.text: Supply becomes vertical

options.label: E
options.text: Supply shifts right

explanation: The number of sellers is a supply determinant; more producers in the market means more total output is available at every given price, shifting the market supply curve rightward.

prompt: A rightward shift of the supply curve means that producers are now willing and able to supply

options.label: A
options.text: Less of the good at every price level

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: More of the good because the price rose

options.label: D
options.text: Less of the good only at lower prices

options.label: E

explanation: A rightward shift of the supply curve indicates an increase in supply - at every given price, producers are willing and able to sell a greater quantity than before. This represents a change in a supply determinant, not a price change.

prompt: A leftward shift of the supply curve means that producers are now willing and able to supply

options.label: A
options.text: More of the good at every price level

options.label: B
options.text: More of the good only at higher prices

options.label: C
options.text: More of the good because input costs fell

options.label: D
options.text: The same quantity at a lower price

options.label: E
options.text: Less of the good at every price level

explanation: A leftward shift of the supply curve indicates a decrease in supply - at every given price, producers are willing and able to sell a smaller quantity than before; this represents an unfavorable change in a supply determinant.

prompt: Which of the following is a determinant of supply that can shift the supply curve?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: Consumer income levels

options.label: C
options.text: The price of inputs used in production

options.label: D
options.text: The price of the good being supplied

options.label: E
options.text: Consumer tastes and preferences

explanation: Input prices are a supply determinant - they affect the cost of production and shift the supply curve when they change. The price of the good itself causes movement along the curve; consumer income, tastes, and number of buyers are demand-side factors.

prompt: If the government imposes a new per-unit tax on the production of cigarettes, what happens to the supply of cigarettes?

options.text: Supply increases because the government collects more revenue

options.label: E
options.text: Supply shifts left as the tax raises costs

explanation: A production tax increases the cost of producing each unit, reducing profitability; producers are willing to supply less at every given price - the supply curve shifts leftward; taxes on producers are a supply determinant.

prompt: If the government provides a subsidy to producers of electric vehicles, what happens to the supply of electric vehicles?

options.label: A
options.text: Supply shifts right as the subsidy lowers costs

options.label: B
options.text: Supply is unchanged because subsidies only affect consumer behavior

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: Supply decreases (shifts left) because subsidies raise production costs

options.label: E
options.text: Supply decreases because the subsidy attracts new competitors

explanation: A government subsidy reduces the effective cost of production for producers, increasing their profitability at every price; this incentivizes them to supply more, shifting the supply curve rightward (increasing supply).

prompt: Producers expect the price of their good to rise significantly next month. How does this expectation most likely affect the CURRENT supply of the good? Assume producers can store existing inventory and current production costs are unchanged.

options.label: A
options.text: Current supply rises from higher output prices today

options.label: B
options.text: Current supply unchanged because storage has no effect

options.label: C
options.text: Current supply falls as sellers hold inventory for later

options.label: D
options.text: Current supply falls because input costs necessarily rise

options.label: E
options.text: Current supply rises as sellers unload inventory early

explanation: Producer expectations about future prices are a supply determinant. If producers expect prices to rise, they have an incentive to reduce current supply (hold back inventory) and sell more next month at the higher price, shifting the current supply curve leftward.

prompt: A drought destroys a significant portion of the corn crop. What happens to the supply of corn?

options.label: A
options.text: Upward movement along supply

options.label: B
options.text: Downward movement along supply

options.label: C
options.text: Supply shifts right

options.label: D
options.text: Supply shifts left

options.label: E
options.text: Supply remains unchanged

explanation: Natural disasters are supply determinants; A drought destroys productive resources (crops), reducing the quantity of corn that can be produced at every price level; the supply curve shifts leftward - a decrease in supply.

prompt: Which of the following correctly distinguishes between a "change in supply" and a "change in quantity supplied"?

options.label: A
options.text: Both terms always mean movements along supply

options.label: B
options.text: Only input costs shift supply; technology causes movements

options.label: C
options.text: Both terms always mean shifts of supply

options.label: D
options.text: Own-price changes shift supply; nonprice changes cause movements

options.label: E
options.text: Own-price changes cause movements; nonprice changes shift supply

explanation: A change in quantity supplied is caused by a change in the good's own price - a movement along the existing supply curve. A change in supply is caused by a non-price determinant (input costs, technology, number of sellers, expectations, taxes/subsidies) - it shifts the entire supply curve.

prompt: A supply schedule shows that as the price of a smartphone rises from $400 to $600, the quantity supplied by producers rises from 500,000 to 800,000 units per month. This relationship is consistent with

options.label: A
options.text: A downward-sloping supply curve showing an inverse price-quantity relationship

options.label: B
options.text: The positive relationship between price and quantity supplied

options.label: C
options.text: A movement along the demand curve

options.label: D
options.text: A shift of the supply curve caused by improved technology

options.label: E
options.text: A shift of the supply curve caused by lower input costs

explanation: As price rises from $400 to $600, quantity supplied rises from 500,000 to 800,000 - price and quantity move in the same direction. This is consistent with the law of supply, which states a positive relationship between price and quantity supplied.

prompt: A market supply curve is derived from individual firm supply curves by

options.label: A
options.text: Averaging quantities at each price

options.label: B
options.text: Multiplying quantities by market prices

options.label: C
options.text: Selecting the most efficient firm

options.label: D
options.text: Adding quantities at each price

options.label: E
options.text: Adding prices at each quantity

explanation: Market supply is derived by horizontal summation of individual firm supply curves; at each price level, the quantities that all individual firms are willing to supply are added together to get total market quantity supplied at that price.

prompt: Two producers — Firm A and Firm B — supply widgets. At $10 per widget: Firm A supplies 50; Firm B supplies 30. At $15 per widget: Firm A supplies 70; Firm B supplies 50. What is the total market quantity supplied at each price?
explanation: Market supply = sum of all individual firm supplies at each price; at $10: 50 + 30 = 80; at $15: 70 + 50 = 120; this horizontal summation gives the market supply schedule.

prompt: Which of the following events would cause a movement ALONG the supply curve for gasoline rather than a SHIFT of the supply curve?

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: The price of gasoline rises, prompting refineries to produce more

options.label: D
options.text: Several refineries permanently close, reducing the number of producers

options.label: E
options.text: The price of crude oil (a key input) rises dramatically

explanation: A change in the price of gasoline itself causes a movement along the existing supply curve; higher gasoline prices make production more profitable, increasing quantity supplied - a movement up and to the right along the curve.

prompt: Corn can be used to produce both ethanol (fuel) and corn tortillas. If the price of ethanol rises sharply, what happens to the supply of corn tortillas?

options.text: Tortilla supply remains unchanged

options.text: Tortilla supply shifts left

options.text: Downward movement along tortilla supply

explanation: Corn is an input common to both ethanol and tortillas. When the price of ethanol rises, producing ethanol becomes more profitable, so corn producers divert more corn to ethanol production; this reduces the availability of corn for tortilla production, shifting the tortilla supply curve leftward.

prompt: A new environmental regulation requires all coal plants to install expensive pollution-control equipment. What is the most likely effect on the supply of electricity from coal plants?

options.label: A

options.text: Supply increases because cleaner electricity is more desirable

options.label: D
options.text: Supply is unchanged because regulations affect only environmental outcomes

options.label: E
options.text: Supply increases because the regulation improves coal plant efficiency

explanation: Regulations that require expensive equipment raise production costs - a supply determinant; higher costs reduce profitability at every price, so producers supply less electricity at every given price; the supply curve shifts leftward.

prompt: A farmer expects the price of soybeans to fall sharply next season. How does this expectation most likely affect the CURRENT supply of soybeans? Assume producers can store existing inventory and current production costs are unchanged.

options.label: E
options.text: Current supply rises because production inputs necessarily become cheaper

explanation: When producers expect future prices to fall, they have an incentive to sell as much as possible NOW at current (higher) prices - increasing current supply and shifting the current supply curve rightward. This is the opposite of expecting prices to rise.

explanation: A leftward shift of the supply curve (from S₁ to S₂) represents a decrease in supply - less is produced at every price. Rising input prices increase production costs, making production less profitable and causing producers to supply less at every given price.

prompt: Why does the supply curve slope upward? Which of the following best explains the positive price-quantity relationship for supply?

prompt: Soybeans and sunflower oil are both produced using the same farmland. If the price of soybeans rises significantly, what happens to the supply of sunflower oil?

prompt: Three firms supply widgets. At $8 per widget: Firm 1 supplies 20; Firm 2 supplies 15; Firm 3 supplies 10. At $12 per widget: Firm 1 supplies 30; Firm 2 supplies 25; Firm 3 supplies 20. What is the total market supply at each price, and which law does this data illustrate?
